paper_title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Modern large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded their context windows, with recent frontier models supporting up to 1M tokens (Gemini Team et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), enabling complex applications such as long-document comprehension, repository-level coding, and test-time reasoning scaling (Wei et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025). However, serving these models at long contexts and large batch sizes is severely bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache (Kwon et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026). Unlike static model weights, the KV cache grows linearly with both sequence length and concurrency, quickly dominating GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as it is repeatedly loaded during decoding (Xia et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). Quantizing the KV cache to low precision effectively compresses its memory footprint and reduces data movement (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024). Recently, 4-bit microscaling formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4 (Rouhani et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025c) have improved low-bit numerical fidelity while enabling native 4-bit matrix multiplications directly on Tensor Cores, delivering 2 or higher throughput than FP8 on modern NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin GPUs (NVIDIA, 2025a) and eliminating the runtime dequantization overhead of low-bit KV caches. Recent works further show that these formats achieve high accuracy and efficiency for weight and activation quantization in training and inference (Cook et al., 2025; Egiazarian et al., 2026), as well as for prefill and non-causal attention (Zhang et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). However, for autoregressive KV cache decoding, fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration, as shown in Figure 1 (right). On the one hand, existing efficient NVFP4 KV cache systems such as TRT-LLM-NVFP4 (NVIDIA, 2025d) directly apply vanilla NVFP4 to the KV cache, causing severe accuracy drops in long-context inference; meanwhile, DeepInfer (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b;a) relies on post-training without considering the underlying quantization error. On the other hand, accuracy-oriented KV quantization algorithms such as TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2026) rely on vector codebooks whose online lookup and reconstruction overhead is inefficient on GPUs, severely degrading decoding throughput. To further push decoding performance, executing attention natively on FP4 Tensor Cores while preserving accuracy poses coupled algorithmic and system challenges. First, at the algorithm level, whereas dequantization-based kernels BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via AlgorithmSystem Co-Design Accuracy-preserving FP4 KV quantization algorithm. We propose microscaling FP4 KV quantization recipe that stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV in average accuracy with NVFP4 (within 1 point with MXFP4) across challenging long-context and reasoning benchmarks, outperforming FP8 KV and prior 4-bit methods, and generalizes across dense and MoE models up to 770B with GQA and MLA attention. In RL post-training rollouts, it closely tracks BF16 KV accuracy, avoiding the degradation of standard NVFP4. Fast native FP4 decoding kernels. Our native FP4 attention kernels keep the accuracy-recipe overhead within 4% and achieve up to 2.99 and 4.01 speedups over BF16 KV at 128K context on B300 and RTX PRO 5000, outperforming TRT-LLM-NVFP4, FlashInfer-XQA-NVFP4, and BitDecoding. High end-to-end serving efficiency. In end-to-end serving, BitDecoding-FP4 shrinks KV cache memory by up to 3.5, cuts decoding latency by up to 1.81, and delivers 2.43.0 higher peak throughput than BF16 KV at 64K128K contexts, matching or exceeding TRT-LLM-NVFP4.

Second, at the system level, simply invoking FP4 Tensor Cores on paged KV caches (Kwon et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) does not automatically yield decoding speedups: as matrix multiplication accelerates, the bottleneck shifts to CUDA-core softmax reductions, and accuracy-preserving quantization steps (e.g., per-tile FP32 rescaling or extra query GEMMs (Zhang et al., 2025b)) stall the decoding pipeline if not co-designed with the kernel. In this paper, we present BitDecoding-FP4, which addresses both challenges through an algorithmsystem co-design for native FP4 KV cache decoding, as illustrated in Figure 1 (left). At the algorithm level, we identify and mitigate the three primary error sources in native FP4 attention: (i) DualResidual Query Quantization represents the query as the sum of two FP4 tensors to suppress logit error from query quantization; (ii) Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 block scales from rounding small long-context softmax probabilities to zero via exponent rescaling and adaptive scale-maximum selection; and (iii) Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static key smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and block-scale search to tame key channel outliers under token-wise quantization. At the kernel level, we remove the softmax bottleneck with transposed softmax that parallelizes reductions across keys and fuses probability quantization into warp-level butterfly shuffles, while stacked query MMA folds the residual query into single narrow FP4 MMA and integrates seamlessly with paged KV caches (Kwon et al., 2023) via device-side control kernel to reduce metadata overhead. sections.title: 4 SYSTEM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION
sections.content: Pairing an FP4 KV cache with native FP4 Tensor Cores substantially reduces the memory footprint and bandwidth traffic of decoding, but turning those savings into wall-clock speedup is non-trivial. In Section 4.1, we identify softmax and on-the-fly probability quantization as the primary execution bottleneck of native FP4 decoding, and propose transposed softmax with fused quantization to remove it. In Section 4.2, we show how Dual-Residual Query Quantization stacks its second query term into the zero padding of the first, so both terms share one narrow FP4 MMA per key tile. Finally, in Section 4.3, we describe how BF16 attention-sink and recent tokens join the FP4 pages in the same decode launch, and how BitDecoding-FP4 integrates into vLLM for online serving. 4.1 Transposed Softmax with Fused Quantization Compute bottleneck from softmax. In FlashAttentionstyle kernels (Dao et al., 2022; Zadouri et al., 2026), the attention score (logit) tile of height is partitioned across softmax threads along the row dimension. For tile of Bk keys and the query heads that share KV head, the conventional layout computes = QK RGBk , so each thread is assigned to query-head row (Figure 5(b)). During decoding, is usually much smaller than the MMA tile height , so most threads sit idle on padded rows, while the few active threads must scan across the Bk keys of their rows in three serial passes: finding the row maximum, computing exp2 and the row sum, and scanning the row again to find each blocks maximum and dynamically quantize to FP4. This per-thread serial work becomes the primary bottleneck of decode attention as the KV cache precision drops: fewer bytes per token raise the arithmetic intensity (Figure 5(a)), but the softmax, rather than the Tensor Cores, sets the ceiling, leaving the FP4 Tensor Cores largely idle. sections.title: 5 EVALUATIONS
sections.content: Our evaluation highlights the following key results: 1) Accuracy: within 0.5 average points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 (within 1 point with MXFP4), ahead of FP8 KV and prior 4-bit methods (Section 5.2). 2) Efficiency: up to 4.01 faster kernels and 3.0 higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV (Section 5.3). 3) Ablation: the contribution of each algorithm and system technique (Section 5.4). 5.1 Experiment Setup Models and Benchmarks. We evaluate BitDecodingFP4 on four models: Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Qwen330B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., 2025), GLM-4.7FP8 (GLM-4.5 Team, 2025), and Hy4-preview (Tencent Hy Team, 2026), covering dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA attention. We evaluate longcontext tasks with LongBench Pro (Chen et al., 2026), MRCR (Vodrahalli et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2025), and RULER-NIAH (Hsieh et al., 2024), and long reasoning with AIME 2024/2025 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2025), and GPQADiamond (Rein et al., 2024). Hardware. Experiments run on NVIDIA B300 (SM103, 288GB) and RTX PRO 5000 (SM120, 72GB) GPUs. Accuracy and system-level evaluations use one B300 (TP=2 for 128K serving), and kernel benchmarks use both. Implementation. We implement BitDecoding-FP4 in CuTe-DSL (NVIDIA, 2025b), built upon FlashAttention4 (Zadouri et al., 2026), and integrate it into vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) as custom PagedAttention backend. Baselines. We compare against two higher-precision references and three 4-bit KV cache methods. BF16 KV is the unquantized upper bound, and FP8 KV is vLLMs FP8 (E4M3) KV cache. For 4-bit, TRT-LLM-NVFP4 (NVIDIA, 2025d) is the native NVFP4 KV cache in vLLM, served by FlashInfers TRT-LLM kernels; TurboQuant-4bit-nc (Zandieh et al., 2026) uses the official vLLM implementation, where for fairness we disable its mixed-precision setup and quantize all layers; and SAW-INT4 (Jia et al., 2026) runs on SGLang. RL Training. To evaluate KV quantization during RL post-training, we follow DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) and run training with BF16 weights, using different KV cache methods for rollout generation and evaluating mean@4 accuracy on problems from DAPO, MATH-500, and AIME 2024. Metadata management for paged KV caches. Serving engines such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) allocate the KV cache in fixed-size blocks on demand, and per-request block table maps its pages to blocks. We store each FP4 page and its block scales in one cache block (Figure 7). The BF16 sink and recent tokens live outside the paged cache, in buffer with one slot si per running request. The engine is unaware of these slots and passes no request identity to the attention kernel, so lightweight control kernel manages them on the device at every step. (1) The kernel identifies the request in each batch row ri by the cache block holding its first page, which stays fixed for the requests lifetime, and matches it against slot table that records the owner and lastseen step of each slot. In Figure 7, row r0 finds its slot s0, while the new request in row r1 takes s2, the least recently seen slot that no row claims; s1 stays with its request, which is not batched in this step. From the sequence lengths, the kernel then splits each row into its FP4 and recent tokens, 384 and 128 for r0, plus the 16 sink tokens, whose FP4 copy in the first page is masked. (2) The decode kernel reads the FP4 pages through the block table and the BF16 tokens through the slot of each row. (3) Once the recent tokens fill page, as for r0, the page is quantized into the cache block already reserved for it, after the last layer has written the token that filled it. Since this metadata never leaves the device, decoding requires no host synchronization and remains compatible with CUDA graphs. sections.title: 6 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Microscaling FP4 for LLMs Microscaling FP4 formats (Rouhani et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025c) have been widely adopted for LLMs in post-training quantization (Cook et al., 2025; Egiazarian et al., 2026), quantizationaware training (Xin et al., 2026), and FP4 training (Castro et al., 2025; Panferov et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2025), though these works quantize only linear layers. For FP4 attention, Attn-QAT (Zhang et al., 2026) relies on quantization-aware training, and MXAttention (Yu et al., 2026) quantizes unnormalized exponentials to preserve softmax normalization under MXFP4. The most closely related post-training work, SageAttention3 (Zhang et al., 2025b), runs both attention matrix multiplications on FP4 Tensor Cores via query/key smoothing (Zhang et al., 2025c;a) and two-level scaling (see algorithmic comparison in Appendix D). However, these methods target prefill, noncausal, or training workloads (e.g., diffusion models) rather than LLM decoding. Low-bit KV Caches for Decoding Recent algorithmic efforts explore 4-bit, 2-bit, and even 1-bit KV cache quantization (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2026; Zandieh et al., 2025): for instance, SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2025) learns rotation matrices to suppress outliers, OScaR (Su et al., 2026) combines canalized rotation with omni-token scaling to address token norm imbalance, and TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2026) pairs random rotation with near-optimal vector quantizers. However, pushing to such extreme bit-widths still incurs non-negligible accuracy degradation on challenging long-context and reasoning tasks. On the systems side, frameworks such as QServe (Lin et al., 2025), SAW-INT4 (Jia et al., 2026), Kitty (Xia et al., 2026), and BitDecoding (Du et al., 2026) accelerate lowbit KV cache decoding. While the original BitDecoding focuses on dequantization optimization, we co-design an accurate microscaling FP4 quantization algorithm with native FP4 Tensor Core kernels that avoid dequantization.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithmsystem codesign that bridges the gap between accuracy-preserving quantization and hardware-native acceleration for microscaling FP4 KV cache decoding. By mitigating the quantization errors of queries, attention probabilities, and keys while eliminating softmax and quantization bottlenecks on FP4 Tensor Cores with paged KV caches, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 average points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4) across models up to 770B, closely tracks BF16 KV in RL rollouts, and achieves up to 4.01 kernel speedup and 2.43.0 higher peak serving throughput. sections.content: End-to-end benchmarks are slow to run and too noisy to separate configurations that are close to BF16 KV. Once quantized model samples different token, its continuation departs from BF16 KVs, so most of the per-sample score difference comes from sampling rather than from quantization. During development, we therefore measure each design choice by how much it changes the models next-token distribution along fixed trajectory shared by all configurations. Measurement. The measurement takes two passes. First, BF16 KV generates reference trajectory = (y1, . . . , yL) for each prompt with the evaluation sampler, and records its next-token distribution pt = pBF16( x, y<t) at every step. Second, each FP4 configuration decodes the same prompts but is teacher-forced along y: at step it computes its own distribution pt = pFP4( x, y<t) from its quantized KV cache, and then emits yt instead of sampling. vLLM logits processor forces the token, so the configuration runs its unmodified serving path, including cache writes and the FP4 decode kernel. The per-token divergence is Dt = (cid:88) vVt pt(v) log pt(v) pt(v) , (9) where Vt holds BF16 KVs 128 most likely tokens at step t, which carry 99.996% of its probability mass on average. We average Dt over the steps of each trajectory and then over trajectories. Because all configurations see exactly the same prefixes, two of them can be compared trajectory by trajectory: we report the paired statistic of their pertrajectory differences, which cancels the large spread in difficulty across prompts. Relation to end-to-end accuracy. Table 3 places the KL of four configurations next to their MRCR accuracy. KL, top-1 mismatch and accuracy rank the four configurations in the same order, and large reductions in KL translate into large accuracy gains: BitDecoding-NVFP4 cuts the KL of TRT-LLM-NVFP4 by 10 and recovers 7.8 of its 10.0-point MRCR gap to BF16 KV. The served model greedily continues each prompt for 256 tokens, so calibration generates only 2K tokens in total. We join the eight prompts and continuations, tile them into one prompt that fills the whole context window (131,071 tokens for 128K window), prefill it once, and accumulate the post-RoPE keys of every layer and KV head; their mean is µk. The text is the models own output, so it matches what the model generates when serving, and tiling lets single prefill cover every position of the window, which matters because RoPE makes the key mean depend on position. As shown in Table 6, Dual-Residual Query Quantization achieves the lowest logit error, reducing the query term to just 1.2% of the total, compared to 42% for smoothing with the token mean and 20% with the stronger GQA mean (the variant shown in Figure 3). Subtracting mean shrinks only the component shared across tokens or heads and still rounds the remainder to FP4 once, whereas our second FP4 term directly quantizes that rounding error itself. Higher efficiency. Smoothing requires extra CUDA-core work and instructions to compute the high-precision correction qki for each key, or extra memory overhead to store precomputed projections per key. In contrast, our second query term stays on the Tensor Cores: stacked into the zero padding of the first (Section 4.2), it only widens the query MMA from to 2G columns, often within padding the MMA computes anyway, and is far more efficient. Higher efficiency. Our constant = 8 folds directly into the exp2 argument (line 10 of Algorithm 1) and cancels in the softmax normalization, adding no extra instructions or output correction. In contrast, two-level scaling changes its FP32 scale at every tile, requiring exact per-tile maximum reductions and per-tile output rescaling on CUDA cores. In our decode implementation of two-level scaling, keeping the FP32 running output in registers for per-tile rescaling also causes severe register spilling, making the kernel 3.026.7 slower than ours across 8K128K contexts and batches 116, and serving decode step 5.0 slower (89.7 vs. 17.8 ms). MXFP4 ADJACENT-EXPONENT BLOCK-SCALE SEARCH In MXFP4 (Rouhani et al., 2023), each block xb of 32 elements shares one unsigned 8-bit power-of-two E8M0 scale sb = 2e (e [127, 127]). Because the largest representable E2M1 magnitude is 6 = 1.5 22, the standard OCP exponent rule sets (10) eocp = log2(max xb) 2. Since max xb [2log2(max xb), 2log2(max xb)+1), dividing by 2eocp maps max xb into [4, 8). Whenever max xb > 6 2eocp, the standard OCP scale clips the block maximum down to 6 2eocp. Conversely, selecting the next power of two, eocp +1, maps max xb into [2, 4) and avoids clipping, at the cost of doubling the quantization step size for the rest of the block. To balance clipping error on the largest elements against rounding error on the interior elements, we evaluate both adjacent exponents for each block, Sb = (cid:8)2eocp, 2eocp+1(cid:9), and select the scale that minimizes the squared reconstruction error in Eq. 6 (breaking ties in favor of 2eocp). Because the round-up exponent log2(max xb/6) is always either eocp or eocp + 1, this two-candidate search is guaranteed to achieve no higher block MSE than either fixed rule.
